enc.title: Choudhuri 1.1: Mass of the Galaxy from the Sun’s orbit
enc.goal: The Sun is about $8$ kpc from the galactic centre and moves on a nearly circular orbit at about $220\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Make a rough estimate of the mass of the Galaxy.

steps.prompt: Which force provides the centripetal acceleration, and which mass counts?
steps.reveal: Gravity of the mass $M$ inside the orbit (for a roughly spherical distribution the outer mass exerts no net force): $\dfrac{v^2}{R}=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}$.

steps.prompt: Solve for $M$ and put in the numbers.
steps.reveal: $M=\dfrac{v^2R}{G}=\dfrac{(2.2\times10^5)^2\,(8\times3.09\times10^{19})}{6.67\times10^{-11}}\approx 1.8\times10^{41}\ \mathrm{kg}\approx 9\times10^{10}\,M_\odot$.
It is the mass inside the solar circle only, about $10^{11}M_\odot$. The flat rotation curve further out (Ch. 6.3) shows that the total mass, dark halo included, is several times larger.

keyPoints: only the mass inside $R$ is measured

enc.title: Choudhuri 1.2: Absolute magnitude and luminosity of a nearby star
enc.goal: A star at a distance of $4$ pc has apparent magnitude $m=2$. Find its absolute magnitude. The Sun has $L_\odot=3.9\times10^{26}$ W and absolute magnitude about $5$: find the luminosity of the star.

steps.prompt: Absolute magnitude: the magnitude the star would have at $10$ pc.
steps.reveal: $M=2-5\log_{10}(0.4)=2+1.99\approx 3.99$. The star is closer than 10 pc, so it would look fainter there ($M>m$).

steps.prompt: Compare with the Sun using the magnitude scale.

steps.reveal: $L\approx 2.54\times3.9\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{W}\approx 9.7\times10^{26}$ W, about $2.5L_\odot$.

keyPoints: distance modulus with the right sign

enc.title: Choudhuri 1.3: Resolution of the GMRT
enc.goal: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope has antennas spread over about $10$ km. Estimate its resolution in arcseconds. How large would an optical telescope have to be for the same resolution in visible light?
given: GMRT works at metre wavelengths (50 MHz to 1.4 GHz, i.e. $\lambda\approx0.2$ to $6$ m)

steps.reveal: An interferometer resolves like a single dish of the size of its longest baseline, $D\approx10^4$ m. Take a typical "metrewave" $\lambda\approx1$ m.
$\theta\approx\lambda/D=10^{-4}$ rad $\approx 20.6^{\prime\prime}$. At the 21 cm line it would be $\approx 4.33^{\prime\prime}$.

$D=\lambda/\theta=5\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}/10^{-4}=5\times10^{-3}$ m: a 5 mm lens. Radio astronomy needs huge apertures because $\lambda$ is $10^6$ times longer (and the atmosphere, not diffraction, limits big optical telescopes to about $1^{\prime\prime}$).

enc.title: Choudhuri 2.3: Saha equation for air-density hydrogen
enc.goal: Hydrogen gas has the density of air at normal conditions, $\rho=1.29\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. With $\chi=13.6$ eV, use the Saha equation (2.29) to calculate the ionization fraction $x$ at different temperatures and plot $x(T)$.
given: Note: Book Fig. and equation numbers refer to Choudhuri; the table was computed with the book constants.

steps.prompt: The density is fixed, the pressure is not. Use the density form of the Saha law.
steps.reveal: With $n_e=n_p=xn$, $n_H=(1-x)n$ and $n=\rho/m_H=7.7\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$: $\dfrac{n_en_p}{n_H}=\dfrac{x^2n}{1-x}=\left(\dfrac{2\pi m_e\kappa_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}e^{-\chi/\kappa_BT}$. This is (2.29) with the pressure written as $P=n\kappa_BT$; the pressure form at fixed $P$ would describe a different gas.

steps.prompt: Solve for $x$ at a few temperatures (a quadratic in $x$).

steps.reveal: $x$ stays tiny up to $\sim10^4$ K and reaches $1/2$ only near $T\approx4\times10^{4}$ K. Ionisation is held back by the high density (recombination is fast); in stellar atmospheres ($n$ much lower) hydrogen ionises near $10^4$ K.

keyPoints: $x(T)$ rises steeply; $x=1/2$ at a few $10^4$ K

enc.title: Choudhuri 2.4: Specific intensity inside a grey atmosphere
enc.goal: Find the specific intensity $I(\tau,\mu>0)$ at an arbitrary optical depth $\tau$ inside a plane-parallel grey atmosphere in the Eddington approximation, with constant flux $F$.

steps.prompt: Substitute the source function into the formal solution.
steps.reveal: $I=\dfrac{3F}{4\pi}\displaystyle\int_\tau^\infty\left(t+\tfrac23\right)e^{-(t-\tau)/\mu}\frac{dt}{\mu}$; put $s=t-\tau$.
$\int_0^\infty e^{-s/\mu}ds/\mu=1$ and $\int_0^\infty s\,e^{-s/\mu}ds/\mu=\mu$, so $I(\tau,\mu)=\dfrac{3F}{4\pi}\left(\tau+\mu+\dfrac23\right)$.

At $\tau=0$ this is (2.66) with $q=2/3$. Limb darkening: $I(0,\mu)/I(0,1)=\frac35(\mu+\frac23)$, the centre is brighter than the limb. Deep inside, $I\to S+\frac{3F}{4\pi}\mu$: nearly isotropic with a small outward excess that carries the flux.

keyPoints: formal solution with the Eddington source function

enc.title: Choudhuri 2.7: Thomson scattering in an ionized "atmosphere"
enc.goal: Fully ionized hydrogen has the density of the Earth’s atmosphere. Using Thomson scattering by free electrons, find the path length after which a light beam is reduced to half its intensity. (Why did matter-radiation decoupling only happen after recombination, §11.7?)

steps.reveal: One electron per proton: $n_e=\rho/m_H=1.29/1.67\times10^{-27}=7.7\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$.
$e^{-n_e\sigma_Ts}=\frac12\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{\ln2}{n_e\sigma_T}=13.5$ m.

A fully ionized gas of air density is opaque after a few tens of metres. Before recombination the Universe was such a fog: photons scattered constantly. Only when the electrons were bound into atoms ($z\approx1100$) did the mean free path become larger than the horizon, and the CMB photons travel freely.

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.1: Thermal versus gravitational energy of the Sun
enc.goal: Estimate the total thermal energy of the Sun from the fact that its internal temperature is of order $10^7$ K. Show that it is of the same order as the rough estimate of the gravitational potential energy.

steps.reveal: Ionized gas, $\mu\approx0.6$: $N=M_\odot/(0.6m_H)\approx2\times10^{57}$.
$E_{\rm th}\approx\frac32N\kappa_B(10^7\ \mathrm K)\approx4.1\times10^{41}$ J.

$|E_G|\approx GM_\odot^2/R_\odot=3.8\times10^{41}$ J: the same order. This is the virial theorem (§3.2.2): $2E_{\rm th}+E_G=0$, i.e. a self-gravitating gas ball in equilibrium must have $\kappa_BT\sim GMm_H/R$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.2: Kelvin–Helmholtz contraction rate
enc.goal: If the Sun produced its energy by slow contraction (Helmholtz and Kelvin), by how much would its radius have to decrease every year to supply the observed luminosity?
given: virial theorem: half of the released gravitational energy is radiated

steps.reveal: $L=\frac12\dfrac{d|E_G|}{dt}=\frac12\dfrac{GM^2}{R^2}\left|\dfrac{dR}{dt}\right|$ (the other half heats the star).
$\left|\dfrac{dR}{dt}\right|=\dfrac{2LR^2}{GM^2}=1.4\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx44.5$ m per year (with $E_G=-\frac35GM^2/R$ for a uniform sphere: $\approx74.2$ m/yr).

steps.prompt: Is that observable, and why is the hypothesis wrong?
steps.reveal: Tens of metres per year is far below what we can measure. The objection is the time scale: $\tau_{KH}\approx|E_G|/2L\approx10^7$ yr, far shorter than the geological age of the Earth.

keyPoints: Kelvin–Helmholtz time $\sim10^7$ yr is too short

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.3: Radiation versus gas pressure in the solar centre
enc.goal: Show that the radiation pressure at the centre of the Sun is negligible compared to the gas pressure, by estimating their ratio.

steps.reveal: $P_{\rm rad}=\frac13a_BT_c^4\approx1.5\times10^{13}$ Pa.
$P_{\rm gas}=\dfrac{\rho_c\kappa_BT_c}{\mu m_H}\approx3.1\times10^{16}$ Pa.
$P_{\rm rad}/P_{\rm gas}\approx4.8\times10^{-4}$. The ratio $\propto T^3/\rho$; for stars on the main sequence it grows with mass (Exercise 5.5), so radiation pressure matters only for massive stars.

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.4: Structure of the solar convection zone
enc.goal: The Sun has a convection zone from $0.7R_\odot$ to the surface. Find how $\rho$, $P$ and $T$ vary in it, assuming (i) (3.22) holds exactly and (ii) the zone contains so little mass that $g=GM_\odot/r^2$.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{d\ln T}{d\ln P}=1-\dfrac1\gamma=\dfrac25$: $P\propto T^{5/2}$ and with the ideal gas $\rho\propto T^{3/2}$ (an adiabat, polytrope $n=3/2$).
Insert hydrostatic equilibrium: $\dfrac{dT}{dr}=-\dfrac25\dfrac{T}{P}\dfrac{GM\rho}{r^2}=-\dfrac25\dfrac{GM\mu m_H}{\kappa_Br^2}$: a constant times $1/r^2$.
$T(r)=\dfrac25\dfrac{GM\mu m_H}{\kappa_B}\left(\dfrac1r-\dfrac1R\right)$, then $\rho=\rho_b\,(T/T_b)^{3/2}$, $P=P_b\,(T/T_b)^{5/2}$.
$T_b=\frac25\times1.4\times10^{7}\ \mathrm K\times(1/0.7-1)\approx2.4\times10^{6}$ K, close to the $2\times10^6$ K of solar models.

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.5: Eddington limit and maximum stellar mass
enc.goal: In very hot stars the opacity is Thomson scattering. Show that $L/M$ must be below a critical value and find it; compare with $L_\odot/M_\odot$. Use (3.45) to estimate the maximum mass for which the outer layers are not blown off.

steps.prompt: Balance radiation force and gravity on a gas element.
steps.reveal: Radiative force per unit mass $\chi F/c=\chi L/(4\pi r^2c)$ must be below $GM/r^2$: $\dfrac LM<\dfrac{4\pi cG}{\chi}$. $R$ cancels.
$\chi=\sigma_T/m_H=0.0398\ \mathrm{m^2kg^{-1}}$, so $(L/M)_{\max}=6.31\ \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$; the Sun has $L_\odot/M_\odot=1.9\times10^{-4}$, about $3.3\times10^{4}$ times less.

$\lambda=L_\odot/M_\odot^3$, so $\left(\dfrac{M_{\max}}{M_\odot}\right)^2=\dfrac{(L/M)_{\max}}{L_\odot/M_\odot}\Rightarrow M_{\max}\approx181M_\odot$. Real upper masses are $\sim100M_\odot$: the order is right.

keyPoints: radiative force $\chi L/4\pi r^2c$ versus gravity

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.6: Distance of the globular cluster M3
enc.goal: From Figures 3.5 and 3.8, estimate the distance of the globular cluster M3.
given: a feature of known absolute magnitude in the cluster’s HR diagram
Note: The magnitudes are typical literature values for M3; check them against Figs. 3.5 and 3.8 of the book.

steps.reveal: Fig. 3.8 is the colour–magnitude diagram of M3 in apparent magnitude. Pick a feature whose absolute magnitude you know from Fig. 3.5 (the HR diagram of nearby stars): the horizontal branch ($M_V\approx+0.6$) or the main sequence at the same colour (main-sequence fitting).
The horizontal branch of M3 lies at $V\approx15.6$: $m-M\approx15.0$, $d=10^{(m-M+5)/5}$ pc $\approx10^{4}$ pc, i.e. about $10$ kpc.
Reading the figures ($\pm0.3$ mag gives $\pm15\%$ in $d$), metallicity differences between cluster and field stars, and interstellar extinction (small for M3, high galactic latitude).

keyPoints: shift between apparent and absolute sequence = distance modulus

enc.title: Choudhuri 3.7: Peak wavelengths of a $9M_\odot$ and a $0.25M_\odot$ star
enc.goal: Make a very rough estimate of the wavelengths at which a star of $9M_\odot$ and a star of $0.25M_\odot$ emit maximum radiation.
given: main-sequence $T_{\rm eff}$ from the HR diagram (Fig. 3.5) or scaling laws

steps.reveal: From the HR diagram: a $9M_\odot$ star is an early B star, $T_{\rm eff}\approx2.2\times10^{4}$ K; a $0.25M_\odot$ star is an M dwarf, $T_{\rm eff}\approx3.4e+03$ K.
$\lambda_{\max}\approx1.3\times10^{-7}$ m (ultraviolet) and $\approx8.5\times10^{-7}$ m (near infrared).

steps.prompt: Why a pure scaling estimate is poor here.
steps.reveal: $L\propto M^3$ with $R\propto M$ gives $T\propto M^{1/4}$, i.e. only $10^{4}$ K for $9M_\odot$: the radius grows more slowly than $M$ and $L$ faster than $M^3$ for massive stars. Reading the HR diagram is the better rough estimate.

keyPoints: $T_{\rm eff}$ from mass via the main sequence
UV for the massive star, near IR for the M dwarf

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.1: Gamow factor from WKB
enc.goal: Nuclei of charges $Z_1e$, $Z_2e$ approach with relative energy $E$; classically they cannot come closer than $r_1$, $E=\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r_1}$. With WKB show $P\propto\exp\left[-2\displaystyle\int_{r_0}^{r_1}\sqrt{\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\left(\frac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}-E\right)}dr\right]$ ($m$ reduced mass, $r_0$ nuclear radius). Evaluate the integral with $r=r_1\cos^2\theta$ for $r_1\gg r_0$ and obtain (4.7).

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}-E=E\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r}-1\right)$, so the exponent is $-2\sqrt{\dfrac{2mE}{\hbar^2}}\displaystyle\int_{r_0}^{r_1}\sqrt{\frac{r_1}{r}-1}\,dr$.

$dr=-2r_1\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{r_1/r-1}=\tan\theta$: $\displaystyle\int=2r_1\int_0^{\theta_0}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=r_1\left[\theta_0-\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\right]$, with $\cos^2\theta_0=r_0/r_1$.
$\theta_0\to\pi/2$: the integral $\to\pi r_1/2$ (correction $-2\sqrt{r_0r_1}$, the small "nuclear radius" term).

Exponent $=-2\sqrt{\dfrac{2mE}{\hbar^2}}\dfrac{\pi}{2}\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0E}=-\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{4\epsilon_0\hbar}\sqrt{\dfrac{2m}{E}}=-\dfrac{1}{2\epsilon_0\hbar}\left(\dfrac m2\right)^{1/2}\dfrac{Z_1Z_2e^2}{\sqrt E}$, which is (4.7). Equivalently $P\propto e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$, $E_G=2mc^2(\pi\alpha Z_1Z_2)^2$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.2: The pp-chain exponent
enc.goal: For two protons, show that the argument of the exponential in the energy generation rate (4.19) becomes the one in (4.25), $-33.8\,(10^6/T)^{1/3}$.

steps.prompt: Where does the 3 and the cube root come from?
steps.reveal: Maximising $e^{-E/\kappa_BT-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$ (Gamow peak) gives $E_0=(E_G(\kappa_BT)^2/4)^{1/3}$ and exponent $-3(E_G/4\kappa_BT)^{1/3}$; $E_G/4=e^4mZ_1^2Z_2^2/(32\epsilon_0^2\hbar^2)$.

steps.prompt: Evaluate the temperature scale for two protons.
steps.reveal: $T_G=\dfrac{e^4(m_p/2)}{32\epsilon_0^2\hbar^2\kappa_B}=1.4\times10^{9}$ K.
$3\left(\dfrac{T_G}{T}\right)^{1/3}=3\left(\dfrac{T_G}{10^6\ \mathrm K}\right)^{1/3}\left(\dfrac{10^6}{T}\right)^{1/3}=33.7\left(\dfrac{10^6}{T}\right)^{1/3}$, i.e. the 33.8 of (4.25).

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.3: Energy generation at the centre of the Sun
enc.goal: The solar centre has $T=1.56\times10^7$ K, $\rho=1.48\times10^5\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $X_H=0.64$, $X_{He}=0.34$, $X_{CNO}=0.015$. Estimate the energy generated per unit volume by the pp chain and the CNO cycle.

steps.reveal: $\varepsilon_{pp}\approx3.1\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$, $\varepsilon_{CNO}\approx6.7\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$.

$\approx460\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ (pp) and $\approx99\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ (CNO): the pp chain dominates in the Sun. Only a few hundred watts per cubic metre, less than a compost heap; the Sun is bright because it is huge.
$d\ln\varepsilon/d\ln T=-\frac23+\frac{33.8}{3}(10^6/T)^{1/3}\approx4$ for pp and $\approx20$ for CNO: CNO wins in hotter (more massive) stars.

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.4: Sound crossing time of the Sun
enc.goal: Make a very rough estimate of the time an acoustic wave travelling radially inward would take to go from one end of the Sun to the other.

steps.reveal: Centre ($1.6\times10^7$ K): $c_s\approx5.9\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; a typical interior temperature $5\times10^6$ K: $c_s\approx3.3\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; near the surface only $\sim10\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
$t\approx2R_\odot/\langle c_s\rangle\approx4.18e+03$ s, about an hour.
Acoustic modes of the Sun (5-minute oscillations) have periods much shorter than this crossing time; their frequencies probe $c_s(r)$ and thus $T(r)$: helioseismology (§4.4).

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.5: Mass lost in the solar wind
enc.goal: Near the Earth the solar wind has $v\approx400\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and about $10$ protons per $\mathrm{cm^3}$. If it always had these values during $4.5\times10^9$ yr, what fraction of its mass has the Sun lost?
given: $\dot M=4\pi r^2nm_pv$ through a sphere of radius 1 AU

steps.reveal: $\dot M=4\pi(1.5\times10^{11})^2\times10^7\times1.67\times10^{-27}\times4\times10^5\approx1.9\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.
$\Delta M=\dot M\times4.5\times10^9\ \mathrm{yr}\approx2.7\times10^{26}$ kg, a fraction $1.3\times10^{-4}$ of $M_\odot$.
$L_\odot/c^2\approx4\times10^9\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$: the Sun loses about twice as much mass to radiation as to the wind, both negligible for its evolution.

enc.title: Choudhuri 4.6: Neutrino mass from SN 1987A
enc.goal: Neutrinos from SN 1987A travelled $55$ kpc and had energies of $6$–$39$ MeV. If the $12$ s spread in arrival times came from different speeds, show that the neutrino mass cannot be much more than about $20$ eV.

steps.reveal: $\Delta t(E)=\dfrac dc\left(\dfrac cv-1\right)\approx\dfrac dc\dfrac{m^2c^4}{2E^2}$.

steps.prompt: Difference between the slowest and fastest neutrinos.
steps.reveal: $\Delta t_{6}-\Delta t_{39}=\dfrac dc\dfrac{m^2c^4}{2}\left(\dfrac1{E_1^2}-\dfrac1{E_2^2}\right)\le12$ s, with $d/c=5.7\times10^{12}$ s.
$mc^2\le\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times12}{(d/c)(1/36-1/1521)\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}}}}\approx12.5$ eV. The emission itself lasts seconds, so the bound is "not much more than" $\sim10$–$20$ eV.

keyPoints: delay $\propto E^{-2}$, use the two extreme energies

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.1: Kinetic-theory pressure (5.1)
enc.goal: Derive $P=\frac13\displaystyle\int vp\,f(p)\,4\pi p^2dp$ (5.1) by counting the particles that hit a unit area of the wall per unit time and the momentum they transfer in elastic collisions. Then find $f(p)$ for a Maxwellian (2.27) and show $P=n\kappa_BT$.
given: $4\pi f(p)p^2dp$ = number of particles per volume with momentum in $[p,p+dp]$, isotropic

steps.prompt: Particles with momentum $p$ moving at angle $\theta$ to the wall normal: how many hit unit area per unit time?
steps.reveal: The fraction moving into $d\theta$ is $\frac12\sin\theta\,d\theta$; their flux onto the wall is $v\cos\theta$ times their density: $4\pi f p^2dp\cdot v\cos\theta\cdot\frac12\sin\theta\,d\theta$.
Elastic reflection reverses the normal component: $2p\cos\theta$.
$P=\displaystyle\int vp\,f\,4\pi p^2dp\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta=\frac13\int vp\,f\,4\pi p^2dp$ (5.1). It holds for any $v(p)$, also relativistic.
$f(p)=n(2\pi m\kappa_BT)^{-3/2}e^{-p^2/2m\kappa_BT}$, $v=p/m$: $P=\dfrac{1}{3m}\displaystyle\int p^2f\,4\pi p^2dp=\dfrac{n\langle p^2\rangle}{3m}=\dfrac{n\cdot3m\kappa_BT}{3m}=n\kappa_BT$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.2: Exact pressure of a degenerate electron gas
enc.goal: Evaluate (5.5), $P=\dfrac{8\pi}{3h^3}\displaystyle\int_0^{p_F}\dfrac{p^4c^2\,dp}{\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_e^2c^4}}$, with $p=m_ec\sinh\theta$ and show $P=\dfrac{\pi m_e^4c^5}{3h^3}f(x)$, $f(x)=x(2x^2-3)\sqrt{x^2+1}+3\sinh^{-1}x$, $x=p_F/m_ec$. Plot $\log P$ against $\log\rho$ and mark the regions of the limits (5.9) and (5.11).

steps.reveal: $dp=m_ec\cosh\theta\,d\theta$, $\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_e^2c^4}=m_ec^2\cosh\theta$, so the integrand becomes $m_e^4c^5\sinh^4\theta\,d\theta$ and $P=\dfrac{8\pi m_e^4c^5}{3h^3}\displaystyle\int_0^{\theta_F}\sinh^4\theta\,d\theta$.

$\sinh^4\theta=\frac18(\cosh4\theta-4\cosh2\theta+3)$, so $\int_0^{\theta_F}=\frac{\sinh4\theta_F}{32}-\frac{\sinh2\theta_F}{4}+\frac{3\theta_F}{8}$. With $x=\sinh\theta_F$: $\sinh2\theta=2x\sqrt{1+x^2}$, $\sinh4\theta=4x\sqrt{1+x^2}(1+2x^2)$, which gives $\frac18f(x)$. Hence $P=\dfrac{\pi m_e^4c^5}{3h^3}f(x)$.
$x\ll1$: $f\approx\frac85x^5$, $P\propto p_F^5\propto\rho^{5/3}$ (5.9). $x\gg1$: $f\approx2x^4$, $P\propto\rho^{4/3}$ (5.11).

$x=1$ when $n_e=\frac{8\pi}{3}(m_ec/h)^3=5.9\times10^{35}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, i.e. $\rho\approx2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ for $\mu_e=2$. On the $\log P$–$\log\rho$ plot the slope bends from $5/3$ to $4/3$ around there.

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.3: The polytropic constants $K_1$, $K_2$ and Fig. 5.1
enc.goal: Carry out all the algebra and numbers to obtain (5.9)–(5.12). Then produce Fig. 5.1 (the $T$–$\rho$ plane divided into regions where the ideal gas, non-relativistic and relativistic degenerate equations of state hold) and justify the procedure.

steps.prompt: Boundaries in the $T$–$\rho$ plane: set the competing pressures equal.
steps.reveal: Ideal gas = non-rel. degenerate: $T=\dfrac{\mu m_HK_1}{\kappa_B}\rho^{2/3}\approx228\,\rho^{2/3}$ K. Non-rel. = rel.: $\rho=(K_2/K_1)^3\approx3.8\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Ideal = rel. degenerate: $T\approx3.6\times10^{5}\,\rho^{1/3}$ K. Radiation = gas: $T=\left(\dfrac{3\kappa_B\rho}{a_B\mu m_H}\right)^{1/3}\approx3.8\times10^{6}\,\rho^{1/3}$ K ($\mu=0.6$, $\mu_e=2$, SI).

steps.prompt: Why is this the right procedure?
steps.reveal: In each region the largest of the candidate pressures is the physical one (the others are small corrections), so the boundary is where two candidates are equal. Example: the solar centre ($\rho=1.5\times10^5$, $T=1.6\times10^7$) lies far above the degeneracy line $T\approx6\times10^5$ K: ideal gas.

keyPoints: justification: equal pressures on a boundary

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.4: Lane–Emden solutions for $n=0$ and $n=1$
enc.goal: Solve $\dfrac1{\xi^2}\dfrac{d}{d\xi}\left(\xi^2\dfrac{d\theta}{d\xi}\right)=-\theta^n$ with $\theta=1$, $\theta'=0$ at $\xi=0$, analytically for $n=0$ and $n=1$ (hint for $n=1$: $\theta=\chi/\xi$ gives $\chi''=-\chi^n/\xi^{n-1}$).
given: $\theta^n\propto\rho$, the surface is the first zero $\xi_1$

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{d}{d\xi}(\xi^2\theta')=-\xi^2\Rightarrow\theta'=-\dfrac\xi3$ (the constant vanishes since $\theta'(0)=0$), $\theta=1-\dfrac{\xi^2}{6}$, $\xi_1=\sqrt6$.
$\xi^2\theta'=\xi\chi'-\chi$, so $\dfrac{d}{d\xi}(\xi^2\theta')=\xi\chi''$ and the equation becomes $\xi\chi''=-\xi^2(\chi/\xi)^n$, i.e. $\chi''=-\chi^n/\xi^{n-1}$.
$\chi''=-\chi\Rightarrow\chi=A\sin\xi+B\cos\xi$; $\theta$ finite at 0 needs $B=0$, $\theta(0)=1$ gives $A=1$: $\theta=\dfrac{\sin\xi}{\xi}$, $\xi_1=\pi$.
Both have $\theta\approx1-\xi^2/6$ near the centre, as every Lane–Emden solution must (expand the equation at small $\xi$).

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.5: Eddington’s standard model: $\beta$ against mass
enc.goal: If the gas pressure is a constant fraction $\beta$ of the total everywhere, show $P_{\rm tot}=\left(\dfrac{3\kappa_B^4}{a_B\mu^4m_H^4}\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}\right)^{1/3}\rho^{4/3}$. For stars of the same $\mu$, show $\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}=CM^2$, find $C$, and show that radiation pressure matters more in massive stars.

steps.reveal: From the gas law $T=\dfrac{\beta P\mu m_H}{\kappa_B\rho}$; put it into $P=\dfrac{a_BT^4}{3(1-\beta)}$: $P^3=\dfrac{3\kappa_B^4}{a_B\mu^4m_H^4}\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}\rho^4$. That is $P=K\rho^{4/3}$: a polytrope of index 3.

steps.prompt: Use the mass of an $n=3$ polytrope (it does not depend on $\rho_c$).
steps.reveal: $K^3=\dfrac{\pi^3G^3M^2}{(4\pi\times2.018)^2}$, so $\dfrac{1-\beta}{\beta^4}=CM^2$ with $C=\dfrac{\pi G^3a_B(\mu m_H)^4}{48\times2.018^2\,\kappa_B^4}$.
$CM_\odot^2\approx4\times10^{-4}$. Solving the quartic: $\beta\approx1$ ($1M_\odot$), $0.966$ ($10M_\odot$), $0.573$ ($100M_\odot$).
$(1-\beta)/\beta^4$ grows as $M^2$: $\beta$ falls with mass, radiation pressure takes over in the most massive stars, which links to the Eddington limit (Exercise 3.5).

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.6: Chandrasekhar’s mass–radius relation (numerical)
enc.goal: Use the exact equation of state of Exercise 5.2 to solve the structure equation (5.13) for different central densities $\rho_c$. Plot $R(M)$ and show that $R\to0$ at the Chandrasekhar mass.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{dM_r}{dr}=4\pi r^2\rho$, $\dfrac{dP}{dr}=-\dfrac{GM_r\rho}{r^2}$, and $\dfrac{d\rho}{dr}=\dfrac{dP/dr}{dP/d\rho}$ with $dP/d\rho$ from $f(x)$.
Start at small $r$ with $\rho=\rho_c$, $M_r=\frac43\pi r^3\rho_c$, integrate outward until $\rho=0$: that gives $R$ and $M=M_r(R)$. Repeat for $\rho_c$ from $10^8$ to $10^{14}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

Low $\rho_c$: $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ (the $n=3/2$ polytrope). As $\rho_c\to\infty$ the electrons are relativistic everywhere, the star becomes an $n=3$ polytrope whose mass is fixed: $M_{\rm Ch}=4\pi\times2.018\,(K_2/\pi G)^{3/2}\approx1.44M_\odot$ for $\mu_e=2$, reached as $R\to0$ (Fig. 5.2).

keyPoints: first-order system with $dP/d\rho$ from the exact EOS

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.7: Spin-up of the collapsing Sun
enc.goal: The Sun rotates in about $27$ days. If it collapsed to a white dwarf conserving angular momentum, what would the rotation period be? And for a neutron star?

steps.reveal: $I\Omega=$ const and $I\propto R^2$ give $P\propto R^2$: $P=P_\odot(R/R_\odot)^2$.
$P\approx27\ \mathrm d\times(6.4\times10^6/6.96\times10^8)^2\approx197$ s, a few minutes.
$P\approx4.8\times10^{-4}$ s, i.e. half a millisecond, near the break-up limit; real pulsars are born slower because most angular momentum is lost on the way (winds, magnetic braking, mass loss).

keyPoints: NS sub-millisecond, as a hint why pulsars spin fast

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.8: Spin-down power and magnetic field of the Crab pulsar
enc.goal: The Crab pulsar has $P=0.033$ s and $P/\dot P=2.5\times10^3$ yr. Estimate its energy loss rate and, using (5.35), its magnetic field.

steps.reveal: $\dot P=P/(2.5\times10^3\ \mathrm{yr})=4.2\times10^{-13}$; $I=1.1\times10^{38}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.
$|\dot E|=I\Omega|\dot\Omega|=\dfrac{4\pi^2I\dot P}{P^3}\approx5.1\times10^{31}$ W, about $10^5L_\odot$: enough to power the Crab nebula.
$B_p=\left(\dfrac{3\mu_0c^3I|\dot\Omega|}{2\pi R^6\Omega^3}\right)^{1/2}\approx8\times10^{8}$ T with $\sin\alpha=1$: about $10^8$–$10^9$ T, typical of young pulsars.

enc.title: Choudhuri 5.9: White-dwarf radius constant and the hottest brown dwarf
enc.goal: Find the proportionality constant in $R\propto M^{-1/3}$ (5.25) using $\xi_1=3.65$, $\xi_1^2|\theta'(\xi_1)|=2.71$ for $n=3/2$. For the limiting brown dwarf ($0.08M_\odot$) held up by electron degeneracy, estimate its radius, the thermal energy gained in its formation and its (uniform) temperature. Nuclear burning needs $T>10^7$ K.

steps.reveal: $\alpha=\dfrac{2.5K_1}{4\pi G}(4\pi\times2.71)^{1/3}M^{-1/3}$, so $R=3.65\,\alpha\approx8.8\times10^{6}\ \mathrm m\,(M/M_\odot)^{-1/3}$ for $\mu_e=2$: an Earth-sized white dwarf.
Then $R\approx4.9\times10^{7}$ m $\approx0.706R_J$ (Jupiter size, as observed for brown dwarfs).
$|E_G|=\frac67GM^2/R\approx2.9\times10^{40}$ J; by the virial theorem half of it stays as heat: $E_{\rm th}\approx1.5\times10^{40}$ J.

$E_{\rm th}=\frac32\dfrac{M}{\mu m_H}\kappa_BT$ with $\mu\approx0.6$: $T\approx4.5\times10^{6}$ K, below $10^7$ K: the contraction is halted by degeneracy before hydrogen can ignite. That is why $\approx0.08M_\odot$ is the dividing line between stars and brown dwarfs.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.1: Star counts with a luminosity function and extinction
enc.goal: A fraction $\Phi(M)dM$ of stars has absolute magnitude in $[M,M+dM]$, absorption adds $a(r)$ magnitudes at distance $r$, and $D(r)$ is the number density. Show that the number of stars per unit apparent magnitude in solid angle $\omega$ is $A(m)=\omega\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\Phi[m+5-5\log_{10}r-a(r)]\,D(r)\,r^2dr$, and that it reduces to (6.3), $A\propto10^{0.6m}$, for equal stars, no absorption and uniform density.

steps.reveal: In $[r,r+dr]$ inside $\omega$ there are $\omega r^2D(r)\,dr$ stars.

steps.prompt: Which of them have apparent magnitude in $[m,m+dm]$?
steps.reveal: Those with $M=m+5-5\log_{10}r-a(r)$; at fixed $r$, $dM=dm$, so the fraction is $\Phi(m+5-5\log_{10}r-a)\,dm$. Summing over shells gives the formula.
$\delta(g(r))$ with $g=m+5-5\log_{10}r-M_0$ picks $r_0=10^{(m-M_0+5)/5}$ with weight $1/|g'(r_0)|=r_0\ln10/5$: $A(m)=\dfrac{\omega D\ln10}{5}r_0^3\propto10^{0.6m}$, which is (6.3).
Deviations from $10^{0.6m}$ tell us about $D(r)$ (the structure of the Galaxy) or $a(r)$ (extinction), the basis of statistical astronomy (Kapteyn).

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.2: Extinction as an exponential
enc.goal: The interstellar medium dims stars in the disk by about $1.5$ magnitudes per kpc. Show that brightness then falls as $e^{-\alpha r}/r^2$ and find $\alpha$.

steps.prompt: Flux reduction factor from $\Delta m=1.5\,r$ (r in kpc).
steps.reveal: $F/F_0=10^{-0.4\times1.5r}=e^{-0.6\ln10\,r}$, times the geometric $1/r^2$.
$\alpha=0.6\ln10\approx1.38\ \mathrm{kpc^{-1}}=4.5\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
The optical depth is $\tau=\alpha r\approx1.4$ per kpc: the galactic centre ($8$ kpc, $\tau\approx11$, about 30 magnitudes) is invisible in visible light.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.3: Oort constants in a Keplerian region
enc.goal: If the gravitational field falls as $r^{-2}$, find the Oort constants $A$ and $B$ (6.21), (6.22). Show that the epicyclic frequency equals the angular velocity and explain its significance.

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{\Theta^2}{R}=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}\Rightarrow\omega\propto R^{-3/2}$, $\dfrac{d\omega}{dR}=-\dfrac32\dfrac\omega R$.
$A=\frac34\omega_0$, $B=A-\omega_0=-\frac14\omega_0$.
$\kappa^2=-4B\omega_0=\omega_0^2$, so $\kappa=\omega_0$.

The radial oscillation has the same period as the orbit: the perturbed orbit closes after one revolution. It is a Kepler ellipse, as it must be for an inverse-square force. In the flat-rotation-curve Galaxy $\kappa=\sqrt2\,\omega$ and orbits are rosettes.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.4: Vertical oscillations through the galactic disk
enc.goal: Model the disk as an infinite slab of constant density. Show that a star displaced vertically oscillates harmonically about the mid-plane. For a mid-plane density of $5\times10^6$ hydrogen atoms per $\mathrm{m^3}$ estimate the period and compare with the orbital period near the Sun.

steps.reveal: $g_z=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dz}=-4\pi G\rho z$ (Gauss’s law with a pillbox, symmetric about $z=0$).
$\ddot z=-4\pi G\rho z$: simple harmonic with $\omega_z^2=4\pi G\rho$.
$\rho=8.4\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$: $P_z=2\pi/\sqrt{4\pi G\rho}\approx7.5\times10^{7}$ yr; the orbit takes $2\pi\times8\ \mathrm{kpc}/220\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\approx2.2\times10^{8}$ yr.
A star crosses the disk a few times per orbit; the Sun is now about $20$ pc above the plane, moving up.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.5: Oscillator strength and the Einstein $B$ coefficient
enc.goal: The oscillator strength of §2.7 satisfies $\dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0m_e}f=h\nu_0B_{lu}$. Show that this makes the discussions of §2.7 and §6.6 consistent.

steps.reveal: Visible lines through cold gas: $h\nu_0\gg\kappa_BT$, so stimulated emission is negligible and the bracket is 1; also $n_l\approx n$.
$\dfrac{h\nu_0}{c}nB_{lu}\phi=\dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0m_ec}nf\phi$ exactly when $\dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0m_e}f=h\nu_0B_{lu}$.
$f$ (classical oscillator language) and $B_{lu}$ (quantum transition rate) are the same physics; the radio case (21 cm, $h\nu_0\ll\kappa_BT$) needs the full bracket of (6.65).

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.6: Three-level atom and population inversion
enc.goal: An atom has levels 1, 2, 3 and no transitions between 2 and 3. Using balance equations like (6.59) and neglecting radiative excitation, show $\dfrac{n_3}{n_2}=\dfrac{g_3(1+A_{21}/n_e\gamma_{21})}{g_2(1+A_{31}/n_e\gamma_{31})}e^{-E_{23}/\kappa_BT}$. Discuss when the populations are inverted.

steps.prompt: Balance for each upper level separately (they only talk to level 1).

steps.reveal: $n_e\gamma\gg A$: the fractions $\to1$ and we recover Boltzmann.

Needs $\dfrac{1+A_{21}/n_e\gamma_{21}}{1+A_{31}/n_e\gamma_{31}}>e^{E_{23}/\kappa_BT}$: level 2 must drain radiatively much faster than level 3 ($A_{21}/\gamma_{21}\gg A_{31}/\gamma_{31}$) at a density where $A_{21}\gtrsim n_e\gamma_{21}$. Collisions pump both levels, but 2 empties quickly: that is the principle behind interstellar masers.

enc.title: Choudhuri 6.7: Rotational lines of CO
enc.goal: CO emits at integer multiples of $115$ GHz. With $I$ the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the molecule, show $E_J=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2I}J(J+1)$ and that the selection rule $\Delta J=-1$ gives the observed spectrum. Estimate the C–O distance.

steps.reveal: A rigid rotor has $E=L^2/2I$ and $L^2=\hbar^2J(J+1)$: $E_J=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2I}J(J+1)$.
$E_J-E_{J-1}=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{I}J$, so $\nu_J=\dfrac{\hbar}{2\pi I}J$: equally spaced, $J\times115$ GHz.

steps.prompt: Moment of inertia and bond length.
steps.reveal: $I=\dfrac{\hbar}{2\pi\times115\ \mathrm{GHz}}=1.5\times10^{-46}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$; with the reduced mass $m=\frac{12\times16}{28}u=1.1\times10^{-26}$ kg, $r=\sqrt{I/m}\approx1.1\times10^{-10}$ m $\approx1.1$ Å.

enc.title: Choudhuri 7.2: Continuity equation from the CBE in cylindrical coordinates
enc.goal: Write the collisionless Boltzmann equation in cylindrical coordinates and, with no assumptions, integrate over velocity space to show $\dfrac{\partial n}{\partial t}+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial r}(n\langle\Pi\rangle)+\dfrac1r\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(n\langle\Theta\rangle)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}(n\langle Z\rangle)+\dfrac{n\langle\Pi\rangle}{r}=0$.

steps.prompt: Integrate the acceleration terms by parts ($f\to0$ at large speed).
steps.reveal: Potential terms and $\frac{\Theta^2}{r}\partial_\Pi f$ integrate to zero (coefficient independent of $\Pi$). But $-\displaystyle\int\frac{\Pi\Theta}{r}\partial_\Theta f\,d^3v=+\frac1r\int\Pi f\,d^3v=\frac{n\langle\Pi\rangle}{r}$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 7.3: Moments of the CBE: fluid equations for stars
enc.goal: From $\partial_tf+v_i\partial_{x_i}f+\dfrac{F_i}m\partial_{v_i}f=0$ show (2) $\partial_t(nm)+\partial_{x_i}(nm\langle v_i\rangle)=0$; multiplying by $mv_j$, (3) $\partial_t(nm\langle v_j\rangle)+\partial_{x_i}(nm\langle v_iv_j\rangle)-nF_j=0$; with $P_{ij}=nm\langle(v_i-\langle v_i\rangle)(v_j-\langle v_j\rangle)\rangle$ show (5) $nm\left(\partial_t\langle v_j\rangle+\langle v_i\rangle\partial_{x_i}\langle v_j\rangle\right)=-\partial_{x_i}P_{ji}+nF_j$. Do (2) and (5) look like fluid equations?

Multiply by $mv_j$ and integrate: $\int mv_jF_i/m\,\partial_{v_i}f=-F_jn$, giving (3).

$\langle v_iv_j\rangle=\langle v_i\rangle\langle v_j\rangle+P_{ij}/nm$. Expand (3) and subtract $\langle v_j\rangle\times$(2): the terms $\langle v_j\rangle[\partial_t(nm)+\partial_i(nm\langle v_i\rangle)]$ cancel, leaving (5).

continuity + Euler analogy and the closure problem

enc.title: Choudhuri 7.4: The King model
enc.goal: Take $f=A\left[e^{-\beta E}-1\right]$ for $E<0$ and $f=0$ for $E>0$, $E=\frac12v^2+\Phi$, $\Phi\to0$ at infinity. Find $\rho(r)$ (it involves the error function), write the equation replacing (7.19), solve it for $-\beta\Phi(0)=12,9,6,3$ and show that $\rho$ vanishes at a finite radius.

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.4: Alfvén waves
enc.goal: Perturb a uniform field $B_0$ in an ideal plasma, neglecting pressure and gravity: $\rho\dfrac{d\mathbf v}{dt}=\dfrac{(\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}$. Show that the perturbations travel along $\mathbf B_0$ at $v_A=B_0/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho}$.

steps.prompt: Linearise with $\mathbf B=B_0\hat e_z+\mathbf b$, transverse $\mathbf v=v_x(z,t)\hat e_x$, $\mathbf b=b_x(z,t)\hat e_x$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.5: Rise speed of a buoyant flux tube
enc.goal: A horizontal flux tube (field $B$, radius $a$) lies in an isothermal atmosphere with constant $g$ and scale height $\Lambda=P/\rho g$. The drag per unit length is $\frac12C_D\rho v^2a$. Show that it rises at the asymptotic speed $v_A\left(\dfrac{\pi a}{\Lambda C_D}\right)^{1/2}$, $v_A=B/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho}$.

steps.reveal: Same $T$ means $\rho\propto P$: $\dfrac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\dfrac{P_e-P_i}{P_e}=\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0P}$.
$\Delta\rho\,g\pi a^2=\dfrac{\rho gB^2}{2\mu_0P}\pi a^2=\dfrac{\pi a^2B^2}{2\mu_0\Lambda}$.
$\dfrac{\pi a^2B^2}{2\mu_0\Lambda}=\dfrac12C_D\rho v^2a\Rightarrow v^2=\dfrac{B^2}{\mu_0\rho}\dfrac{\pi a}{\Lambda C_D}$, the stated result.
Magnetic buoyancy brings tubes generated by the solar dynamo to the surface, where they form sunspots.

enc.title: Choudhuri 8.6: Relativistic Fermi acceleration
enc.goal: (Special relativity.) A relativistic particle moving in one dimension is reflected by reflectors moving with speeds $\pm U$. Show that the average energy gain per collision is (8.44), $\Delta E_{\rm ave}=4\left(\dfrac Uc\right)^2E$.
given: Lorentz transformation of energy for $v\approx c$: $E'=\gamma E(1\pm\beta)$, $\beta=U/c$

steps.reveal: Transform into the reflector frame, reverse the momentum, transform back: $E_+=\gamma^2(1+\beta)^2E=\dfrac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}E$.
$E_-=\dfrac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}E$.
Head-on collisions are more frequent: rates $\propto c+U$ and $c-U$, probabilities $\frac{1\pm\beta}2$.

$\Delta E_{\rm ave}=\dfrac{1+\beta}2\dfrac{2\beta}{1-\beta}E-\dfrac{1-\beta}2\dfrac{2\beta}{1+\beta}E=\dfrac{4\beta^2}{1-\beta^2}E=4\gamma^2\beta^2E\approx4\left(\dfrac Uc\right)^2E$: second-order Fermi acceleration.

keyPoints: energy after head-on and overtaking reflections

enc.goal: From $\omega^2=\omega_p^2+k^2c^2$ (8.82) show $v_{gr}=c\sqrt{1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2}$. enc.title: Choudhuri 9.1: Total light of a de Vaucouleurs galaxy
enc.goal: An elliptical galaxy appears circular with the de Vaucouleurs profile $I(r)=I_e\exp\left\{-7.67\left[(r/r_e)^{1/4}-1\right]\right\}$ (9.2). Show that the total light $\int_0^\infty I\,2\pi r\,dr=7.22\pi r_e^2I_e$, and that exactly half comes from within $r_e$.

Fraction $=\gamma(8,b)/7!=0.5$: one half. That is why $b=7.67$: it is chosen so that $r_e$ is the half-light (effective) radius.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.2: Faber–Jackson slope from Fig. 9.5
enc.goal: From Figure 9.5 argue that $\sigma\propto L^\alpha$ and estimate $\alpha$.
given: on a log–log plot a power law is a straight line with slope $\alpha$
Note: Read the actual points in Fig. 9.5 of the book; the slope there should come out near $1/4$.

steps.reveal: Plot (or read) $\log\sigma$ against $\log L$ (or absolute magnitude, $\log L=-0.4M+$ const): the ellipticals lie along a straight band.
Over a factor $\sim100$ in $L$ (5 magnitudes) $\sigma$ grows by a factor $\sim3$: $\alpha\approx\log3/\log100\approx0.25$, i.e. $L\propto\sigma^4$ (Faber–Jackson).
Virial theorem $\sigma^2\propto M/R$ with a constant mass-to-light ratio and constant surface brightness ($L\propto R^2$) gives $L\propto\sigma^4$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.3: Maximum superluminal motion
enc.goal: A jet blob moves at $0.98c$. At what angle to the line of sight is the apparent superluminal motion largest, and what is the maximum apparent transverse velocity?

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1-\beta\cos\theta}=0\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\beta$.
$\theta=\arccos0.98\approx11.5^\circ$; $v_{\rm app,max}=\beta\gamma c=0.98\times5.03\,c\approx4.92c$.
The blob almost catches up with its own light: emission times are compressed by $1-\beta\cos\theta$, so the projected motion looks faster than $c$ though nothing moves faster than light.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.4: Synchrotron electrons in a radio jet
enc.goal: With $B\sim10^{-10}$ T in jets, estimate $\gamma$ of electrons emitting synchrotron radio waves and their cooling time from (8.59). Compare with the travel time over a $1$ Mpc jet at $0.1c$. Must the electrons be re-accelerated in the jet?

steps.reveal: $\nu_g=2.8$ Hz, so $\gamma\approx\sqrt{10^9/\nu_g}\approx1.9\times10^{4}$.
$t=\dfrac{\gamma m_ec^2}{P}=\dfrac{m_ec}{\frac43\sigma_T\gamma U_B}\approx1.3\times10^{9}$ yr, with $U_B=4\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.
$1\ \mathrm{Mpc}/0.1c\approx3.3\times10^{7}$ yr: shorter than the synchrotron cooling time.

Synchrotron losses alone would let nucleus-accelerated electrons reach the lobes. But inverse Compton scattering on the CMB acts like a field with $U_{\rm CMB}=4.2\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ (10 times $U_B$), cutting the lifetime to $\approx1.1\times10^{8}$ yr; with stronger fields in the lobes and adiabatic losses, in-situ acceleration (shocks, hot spots) is in fact needed.

enc.title: Choudhuri 9.5: Are galaxy clusters virialized?
enc.goal: Estimate the time a galaxy takes to cross a cluster of galaxies and the relaxation time. A cluster is clearly not relaxed, but the virial theorem only needs it to be virialized. Are typical clusters virialized?

steps.reveal: $T_{\rm cross}=R/v\approx9.8\times10^{8}$ yr, about $10^9$ yr.
$T_{\rm rel}\approx NT_{\rm cross}\approx9.8\times10^{11}$ yr, far longer than the age of the Universe: two-body encounters have not relaxed the cluster.

The age ($\sim10^{10}$ yr) is about ten crossing times: enough for violent relaxation to bring the system into a steady state, so rich clusters are roughly virialized (supported by their smooth X-ray gas). Young, irregular clusters with substructure are not, and the virial mass there is uncertain.

keyPoints: virial equilibrium needs only a few crossing times

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.1: Density parameter independent of $h$
enc.goal: Distances from Hubble’s law scale as $h^{-1}$. If the mean density comes from virial masses of galaxy clusters, show that the density parameter is independent of the uncertainty in $H_0$.

steps.reveal: $\sigma$ is measured (redshifts): no $h$. $R=\theta d\propto h^{-1}$, so $M\propto h^{-1}$. The number of clusters per unit volume $\propto d^{-3}\propto h^3$.
$\rho=n_{\rm cl}M\propto h^3h^{-1}=h^2$ (equivalently, $M/L\propto h$ and the luminosity density $\propto h$).
$\Omega=\rho/\rho_c\propto h^2/h^2$: independent of $h$. That is why $\Omega_{M,0}\approx0.3$ was robust while $H_0$ was still disputed.

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.2: Age of the Universe when quasar light left
enc.goal: For quasars at $z=1$ and $z=4$, find the age of the Universe (as a fraction of today’s) when the light left, for $\Omega_{M,0}=1$. Estimate the errors if instead $\Omega_{M,0}=0.5$ or $1.5$ (matter only).

steps.reveal: Integrating numerically: $t/t_0=0.39$ and $0.106$, i.e. $10.2\%$ and $18.3\%$ larger than the EdS estimate.
The fraction depends only weakly on $\Omega$; the error grows with $z$ because the curvature term changes the early expansion history relative to today.

enc.title: Choudhuri 10.3: Age against $\Omega_{M,0}$ (Fig. 10.6)
enc.goal: Assuming a matter-dominated Universe, calculate numerically the age for different $\Omega_{M,0}$ and reproduce Figure 10.6.

steps.reveal: Friedmann with $\rho\propto a^{-3}$ and curvature fixed by $\Omega_{M,0}$: $\dot a=H_0\sqrt{\Omega_{M,0}/a+1-\Omega_{M,0}}$, and $t_0=\int_0^1da/\dot a$.
From $12.5$ Gyr ($\Omega=0.1$) down to $9.31$ Gyr ($\Omega=1$): younger than the oldest globular clusters for $\Omega=1$, the old "age problem" solved by $\Omega_\Lambda$.

enc.goal: If $n+\nu_e\leftrightarrow p+e^-$ had dropped below the expansion rate only at $T\approx0.4$ MeV, what would the helium abundance be?

steps.reveal: $n_n/n_p=e^{-1.29/0.4}\approx0.0398$ (instead of 0.20 at 0.8 MeV).
$Y\approx\dfrac{2\times0.0398}{1+0.0398}\approx0.0765$, an upper bound; neutron decay before nucleosynthesis lowers it further.

$Y$ is exponentially sensitive to the freeze-out temperature, which is set by the weak rate versus $H$. The observed $Y\approx0.25$ therefore tests the weak interaction and the expansion rate (e.g. the number of neutrino species).

enc.title: Choudhuri 11.3: Chemical potentials of electrons and positrons
enc.goal: Before $e^+e^-$ annihilation there were slightly more electrons than positrons. Show that their chemical potentials must then be non-zero, and explain how to calculate them.

steps.reveal: With $\mu=0$ the Fermi–Dirac distributions of $e^-$ and $e^+$ are identical, so $n_-=n_+$. An excess needs $\mu_->0$; the pair equilibrium with photons ($\mu_\gamma=0$) forces $\mu_+=-\mu_-$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 11.6: Growth of a density perturbation, $\delta\propto t^{2/3}$
enc.goal: A spherical shell at $a(t)$ is perturbed to $a+l$. Show $\ddot l=\dfrac{2GM}{a^3}l=\dfrac{8\pi G}3\rho l$. With $\delta=\delta\rho/\rho=-3l/a$ and a marginally critical background, derive $\ddot\delta+\dfrac4{3t}\dot\delta-\dfrac2{3t^2}\delta=0$ and show that $\delta\propto t^{2/3}$ solves it.

$\delta=t^s$: $s(s-1)+\frac43s-\frac23=0\Rightarrow s=\frac23$ or $s=-1$. The growing mode $\delta\propto t^{2/3}\propto a$: perturbations grow only like the scale factor, so from $\delta\sim10^{-5}$ at $z=1100$ they reach $\sim10^{-2}$ today without dark matter (structure-formation argument for dark matter).

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.1: Curvature of three 2D metrics
enc.goal: Work out the Christoffel symbols, Riemann and Ricci tensors and the scalar curvature for $ds^2=dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$, $ds^2=a^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$ and $ds^2=a^2(d\chi^2+\sinh^2\chi\,d\eta^2)$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-r$, $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=1/r$; $R^r{}_{\theta r\theta}=\partial_r\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}-\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}\Gamma^\theta_{\theta r}\ldots=-1+1=0$: flat, $R=0$ (only the coordinates are curved).

$\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\cot\theta$; $R_{\theta\phi\theta\phi}=a^2\sin^2\theta$, $R_{\theta\theta}=1$, $R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta$, $R=\dfrac2{a^2}$.
Same with $\sin\to\sinh$: $\Gamma^\chi_{\eta\eta}=-\sinh\chi\cosh\chi$, $\Gamma^\eta_{\chi\eta}=\coth\chi$; $R_{\chi\chi}=-1$, $R_{\eta\eta}=-\sinh^2\chi$, $R=-\dfrac2{a^2}$.
Constant curvature $K=R/2=+1/a^2,0,-1/a^2$: the 2D analogues of closed, flat and open Robertson–Walker spaces (the sign convention of the book fixes the sign of $R$).

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.2: Covariant derivatives do not commute
enc.goal: Show that two covariant derivatives in general do not commute, and for a contravariant vector $\left(\dfrac{D}{Dx^k}\dfrac{D}{Dx^l}-\dfrac{D}{Dx^l}\dfrac{D}{Dx^k}\right)A^i=-R^i{}_{mlk}A^m$ (book sign convention).

steps.reveal: $A^i{}_{;l;k}=\partial_k(\partial_lA^i+\Gamma^i_{ml}A^m)+\Gamma^i_{nk}(\partial_lA^n+\Gamma^n_{ml}A^m)-\Gamma^n_{lk}A^i{}_{;n}$.

$\partial_k\partial_lA^i$ and $\Gamma^n_{lk}A^i{}_{;n}$ are symmetric and cancel; the terms $\Gamma\,\partial A$ cancel crosswise. What is left multiplies $A^m$: $\left(\partial_k\Gamma^i_{ml}-\partial_l\Gamma^i_{mk}+\Gamma^i_{nk}\Gamma^n_{ml}-\Gamma^i_{nl}\Gamma^n_{mk}\right)A^m$.

With the book’s definition (12.37), $R^i{}_{mlk}=\partial_l\Gamma^i_{mk}-\partial_k\Gamma^i_{ml}+\Gamma^n_{mk}\Gamma^i_{nl}-\Gamma^n_{ml}\Gamma^i_{nk}$, the bracket is exactly $-R^i{}_{mlk}$. Since $\frac{D}{Dx^k}\frac{D}{Dx^l}A^i=A^i{}_{;l;k}$, this is the stated result. Derivatives commute only where the curvature vanishes.

Riemann tensor emerges, sign by convention

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.3: Symmetries of $R_{iklm}$ and the contracted Bianchi step
enc.goal: From (12.37) build $R_{iklm}=g_{in}R^n{}_{klm}$, show $R_{iklm}=\frac12(\partial_k\partial_lg_{im}+\partial_i\partial_mg_{kl}-\partial_k\partial_mg_{il}-\partial_i\partial_lg_{km})+g_{np}(\Gamma^n_{kl}\Gamma^p_{im}-\Gamma^n_{km}\Gamma^p_{il})$, deduce $R_{iklm}=-R_{kilm}=-R_{ikml}=R_{lmik}$, and prove $g^{im}R^n{}_{ilm}=R^n{}_l$ (needed for $\nabla_kG^{ik}=0$).

steps.reveal: $g_{in}\partial_k\Gamma^n_{lm}=\partial_k\Gamma_{i,lm}-\Gamma^n_{lm}\partial_kg_{in}$; the second derivatives of $g$ come from $\partial\Gamma_{i,lm}=\frac12\partial(\partial g+\partial g-\partial g)$, the rest combine into the quadratic $\Gamma\Gamma$ terms.

Read them off: swapping $i\leftrightarrow k$ or $l\leftrightarrow m$ flips the sign of both the derivative and $\Gamma\Gamma$ parts; swapping the pairs $(ik)\leftrightarrow(lm)$ leaves them unchanged (check in a locally geodesic frame where $\Gamma=0$).

$g^{im}R^n{}_{ilm}=g^{im}g^{nk}R_{kilm}$. Pair symmetry and then both antisymmetries: $R_{kilm}=R_{lmki}=-R_{mlki}=R_{mlik}$. Contracting the first and third index with $g^{im}$ gives $g^{im}R_{mlik}=R^i{}_{lik}=R_{lk}$ by (12.41), and $R_{lk}=R_{kl}$. Hence $g^{im}R^n{}_{ilm}=g^{nk}R_{kl}=R^n{}_l$.

keyPoints: lowering the index of the Riemann tensor

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.4: Geodesic deviation
enc.goal: For two neighbouring geodesics $x^i(s)$ and $x^i(s)+\delta x^i(s)$ show $\dfrac{D^2}{Ds^2}\delta x^i=-R^i{}_{klm}\delta x^l\dfrac{dx^k}{ds}\dfrac{dx^m}{ds}$ (book sign convention).

steps.prompt: Subtract the geodesic equations to first order.
steps.reveal: $\delta\ddot x^i+\partial_m\Gamma^i_{kl}\delta x^m\dot x^k\dot x^l+2\Gamma^i_{kl}\dot x^k\delta\dot x^l=0$.

steps.prompt: Rewrite with covariant derivatives along the curve.
steps.reveal: $\dfrac{D\delta x^i}{Ds}=\delta\dot x^i+\Gamma^i_{kl}\dot x^k\delta x^l$; differentiate again and use the geodesic equation to remove $\ddot x$.

All terms combine into $\left(\partial_l\Gamma^i_{km}-\partial_m\Gamma^i_{kl}+\Gamma\Gamma-\Gamma\Gamma\right)\dot x^k\dot x^m\delta x^l$, the Riemann tensor: the stated equation. Physics: tidal acceleration between free particles; in Newtonian terms $\ddot{\delta x}_i=-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi\,\delta x_j$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.5: Great circles are geodesics, other latitude circles are not
enc.goal: Prove that the equator of a sphere is a geodesic, but any other circle of constant latitude is not.

steps.reveal: $\ddot\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\phi^2=0$.
Then $\ddot\theta=0$, so we need $\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0\dot\phi^2=0$: only $\theta_0=\pi/2$ works (the poles are trivial).

$\ddot\phi+2\cot\theta\dot\theta\dot\phi=0$ holds for constant $\theta$ and constant $\dot\phi$. So the equator is a geodesic; a latitude circle needs a force pulling towards the pole axis: an airplane flying "due east" at $60^\circ$ N is constantly turning.

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.6: Metric of a rotating frame
enc.goal: With $ds^2=-c^2dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$ and the rotating coordinates $t'=t$, $z'=z$, $x'=x\cos\Omega t+y\sin\Omega t$, $y'=-x\sin\Omega t+y\cos\Omega t$, find $g_{ik}$ and $g^{ik}$ in the rotating frame and verify $g^{ik}g_{km}=\delta^i_m$.

steps.reveal: $dx=\cos\Omega t\,dx'-\sin\Omega t\,dy'-\Omega y\,dt$, $dy=\sin\Omega t\,dx'+\cos\Omega t\,dy'+\Omega x\,dt$ ($x,y$ expressed through $x',y'$). Then $dx^2+dy^2=dx'^2+dy'^2+2\Omega(x'dy'-y'dx')dt+\Omega^2(x'^2+y'^2)dt^2$.

$ds^2=-\left(c^2-\Omega^2(x'^2+y'^2)\right)dt^2+2\Omega x'dy'dt-2\Omega y'dx'dt+dx'^2+dy'^2+dz'^2$: $g_{tt}=-(c^2-\Omega^2\varrho^2)$, $g_{tx}=-\Omega y'$, $g_{ty}=\Omega x'$, $g_{xx}=g_{yy}=g_{zz}=1$.

$g^{tt}=-1/c^2$, $g^{tx}=-\Omega y'/c^2$, $g^{ty}=\Omega x'/c^2$, $g^{xx}=1-\Omega^2y'^2/c^2$, $g^{yy}=1-\Omega^2x'^2/c^2$, $g^{xy}=\Omega^2x'y'/c^2$, $g^{zz}=1$. Multiplying out $g^{ik}g_{km}$ gives $\delta^i_m$ (e.g. $g^{tt}g_{tt}+g^{tx}g_{xt}+g^{ty}g_{yt}=\frac{c^2-\Omega^2\varrho^2}{c^2}+\frac{\Omega^2y^2}{c^2}+\frac{\Omega^2x^2}{c^2}=1$).
$g_{tt}$ vanishes at $\varrho=c/\Omega$ (light cylinder); the off-diagonal $g_{ti}$ produce the Coriolis force. The space is still flat (all Riemann components zero).

enc.title: Choudhuri 12.7: Einstein tensor of the weak-field metric
enc.goal: For $ds^2=-\left(1+\dfrac{2\Phi}{c^2}\right)c^2dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$ (non-relativistic particle in a weak field), calculate $G_{xx}$ and check the $xx$ component of Einstein’s equation. If it fails, how do you account for it?
given: to first order in $\Phi$; static field
$T_{ik}$ of dust: only $T_{tt}=\rho c^2$ (in these units)

steps.reveal: With $x^0=ct$ and $h_{00}=-2\Phi/c^2$ the linearised Ricci tensor gives $R_{00}=\nabla^2\Phi/c^2$, $R_{ij}=-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi/c^2$, so $R=-R_{00}+R_{ii}=-2\nabla^2\Phi/c^2$ (signature $-+++$).
$G_{xx}=R_{xx}-\frac12R=\dfrac{1}{c^2}\left(\nabla^2\Phi-\partial_x^2\Phi\right)=\dfrac{1}{c^2}(\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2)\Phi\neq0$ inside matter.
$T_{xx}=P\approx0$ for slow matter, but $G_{xx}\ne0$: the equation fails.

The metric is incomplete: at the same order the spatial part also changes, $g_{ij}=(1-2\Phi/c^2)\delta_{ij}$. With it $G_{ij}=0$ and only the $tt$ equation survives, giving $\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho$. The given metric reproduces particle motion (only $g_{tt}$ matters for slow particles), but not light bending, which needs the spatial part too (factor 2 in the deflection).

keyPoints: missing spatial part of the metric

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.1: Lengths, areas and volumes in a curved static metric
enc.goal: For $ds^2=-(1-Ar^2)dt^2+(1-Ar^2)^{\pm1}dr^2+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta d\phi^2)$ calculate (a) the proper radial distance from $r=0$ to $r=R$, (b) the area of the sphere $r=R$, (c) the 3-volume inside it, (d) the 4-volume of the tube between two $t=$ const surfaces separated by $T$.
given: Note: Our text copy shows $g_{rr}=1-Ar^2$; the superscript $-1$ may have been lost. Both versions are solved: use the one printed in your book.

steps.reveal: $\sqrt{g_{\theta\theta}g_{\phi\phi}}=r^2\sin\theta$: $4\pi R^2$ in both cases ($r$ is defined by the area).

(a) $\displaystyle\int_0^R\frac{dr}{\sqrt{1-Ar^2}}=\frac{\arcsin(\sqrt AR)}{\sqrt A}$ ($>R$). (c) $4\pi\displaystyle\int_0^R\frac{r^2dr}{\sqrt{1-Ar^2}}=\frac{2\pi}{A^{3/2}}\left[\arcsin(\sqrt AR)-\sqrt AR\sqrt{1-AR^2}\right]$. (d) $\sqrt{-g}=r^2\sin\theta$: $\frac43\pi R^3T$.

(a) $\frac12\left[R\sqrt{1-AR^2}+\frac{\arcsin(\sqrt AR)}{\sqrt A}\right]$ ($<R$). (c) $4\pi\int_0^Rr^2\sqrt{1-Ar^2}dr$. (d) $\sqrt{-g}=(1-Ar^2)r^2\sin\theta$: $4\pi T\left(\frac{R^3}3-\frac{AR^5}5\right)$.
All reduce to the flat results $R$, $4\pi R^2$, $\frac43\pi R^3$, $\frac43\pi R^3T$.

keyPoints: area is $4\pi R^2$ by definition of $r$

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.2: Schwarzschild solves the vacuum equations
enc.goal: Show that the Schwarzschild metric (13.13) satisfies all components of Einstein’s vacuum equation for $r\neq0$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^t_{tr}=\alpha'$, $\Gamma^r_{tt}=c^2\alpha'e^{2(\alpha-\beta)}$, $\Gamma^r_{rr}=\beta'$, $\Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}=-re^{-2\beta}$, $\Gamma^r_{\phi\phi}=-re^{-2\beta}\sin^2\theta$, $\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}=\Gamma^\phi_{r\phi}=1/r$, $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\cot\theta$.

$R_{tt}\propto\alpha''+\alpha'^2-\alpha'\beta'+\frac2r\alpha'$, $R_{rr}=-\alpha''-\alpha'^2+\alpha'\beta'+\frac2r\beta'$, $R_{\theta\theta}=1-e^{-2\beta}\left[1+r(\alpha'-\beta')\right]$, $R_{\phi\phi}=\sin^2\theta R_{\theta\theta}$.

$e^{2(\beta-\alpha)}R_{tt}/c^2+R_{rr}=\frac2r(\alpha'+\beta')=0\Rightarrow\alpha=-\beta$ (with flat infinity). Then $R_{\theta\theta}=0$ gives $(re^{2\alpha})'=1$, $e^{2\alpha}=1-\dfrac{2GM}{c^2r}$: exactly (13.13); with it $R_{tt}=R_{rr}=0$ too.

keyPoints: Christoffel symbols of the static spherical metric

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.3: Newtonian orbits from the Schwarzschild orbit equation
enc.goal: Neglecting the relativistic term, substitute $u_0=\frac1p(1+\epsilon\cos\phi)$ (13.32) into (13.28), $l^2\left(\frac{du}{d\phi}\right)^2=e^2-1-2V_{\rm eff}(u)$, to show $\epsilon=\sqrt{1+\dfrac{(e^2-1)l^2}{M^2}}$, the condition for an ellipse, $a=\dfrac{l^2}{M(1-\epsilon^2)}$ and $\dfrac{e^2-1}2=-\dfrac M{2a}$ ($G=c=1$). Meaning of the last result?

steps.reveal: $\dfrac{du}{d\phi}=-\dfrac\epsilon p\sin\phi$: $\dfrac{l^2\epsilon^2}{p^2}\sin^2\phi=e^2-1+\dfrac{2M}p(1+\epsilon\cos\phi)-\dfrac{l^2}{p^2}(1+\epsilon\cos\phi)^2$.

$\cos\phi$ terms: $\dfrac{2M\epsilon}p=\dfrac{2l^2\epsilon}{p^2}\Rightarrow p=\dfrac{l^2}M$. Constant terms: $\dfrac{l^2\epsilon^2}{p^2}=e^2-1+\dfrac{2M}p-\dfrac{l^2}{p^2}\Rightarrow\epsilon^2=1+\dfrac{(e^2-1)l^2}{M^2}$.

$\epsilon<1\Leftrightarrow e^2<1$ (bound). Then $r_{\min,\max}=p/(1\pm\epsilon)$, $a=\dfrac{p}{1-\epsilon^2}=\dfrac{l^2}{M(1-\epsilon^2)}$, and $\dfrac{e^2-1}{2}=\dfrac{M^2(\epsilon^2-1)}{2l^2}=-\dfrac M{2a}$.

$e$ is the conserved energy per unit rest energy, so $\frac{e^2-1}2\approx e-1$ is the Newtonian energy per unit mass: $E=-\dfrac{GM}{2a}$, the Kepler result that the energy depends only on the semimajor axis.

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.4: Perihelion of Mercury and light bending by the Sun
enc.goal: (a) Calculate the perihelion precession of Mercury in arcseconds per century ($a=5.79\times10^7$ km, $\epsilon=0.206$, $P=88.0$ d). (b) Evaluate the maximum deflection of light by the Sun.

steps.reveal: $\Delta\phi=\dfrac{6\pi\times1.33\times10^{20}}{9\times10^{16}\times5.79\times10^{10}\times(1-0.206^2)}\approx5\times10^{-7}$ rad.
$415$ orbits per century: $\approx42.9^{\prime\prime}$, the famous $43^{\prime\prime}$ unexplained by Newtonian perturbations.

steps.prompt: Light deflection at the solar limb.
steps.reveal: $\delta=\dfrac{4GM_\odot}{c^2R_\odot}\approx1.75^{\prime\prime}$, twice the "Newtonian" value; confirmed in the 1919 eclipse.

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.5: Escape cone of light near a black hole
enc.goal: Light is emitted at $r_i$ with $2M<r_i<3M$ ($G=c=1$) at angle $\alpha$ to the radial direction. Show it escapes only if $\sin\alpha<\dfrac{3\sqrt3M}{r_i}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)^{1/2}$, so at $r=2M$ only radial light escapes.
given: photon orbit: $\left(\dfrac{du}{d\phi}\right)^2=\dfrac1{b^2}-u^2(1-2Mu)$, maximum of $u^2(1-2Mu)$ at $r=3M$ equals $\dfrac1{27M^2}$

steps.prompt: Angle measured by a static observer.
steps.reveal: Proper radial and tangential distances: $d\ell_r=\dfrac{dr}{\sqrt{1-2M/r}}$, $d\ell_\phi=r\,d\phi$, so $\tan\alpha=\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)^{1/2}r_i\left(\dfrac{d\phi}{dr}\right)_i$ (the hint).

The photon orbit gives $\left(\dfrac{dr}{d\phi}\right)^2=r^4\left[\dfrac1{b^2}-\dfrac1{r^2}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}r\right)\right]$. Then $\tan^2\alpha=\dfrac{1-2M/r_i}{r_i^2/b^2-(1-2M/r_i)}$ and $\sin^2\alpha=\dfrac{\tan^2\alpha}{1+\tan^2\alpha}=\dfrac{b^2}{r_i^2}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)$, i.e. $\dfrac1{b^2}=\dfrac{1-2M/r_i}{r_i^2\sin^2\alpha}$.

Emitted inside the photon sphere ($r_i<3M$) moving outward, the photon escapes only if it passes over the barrier: $\dfrac1{b^2}>\dfrac1{27M^2}$, i.e. $\sin^2\alpha<\dfrac{27M^2}{r_i^2}\left(1-\dfrac{2M}{r_i}\right)$: the stated cone.
At $r_i\to2M$ the right side $\to0$: only exactly radial light escapes; the escape cone closes.

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.6: Static weak field is not a transverse-traceless wave
enc.goal: Far from a spherical star the field is weak. (a) Find $h_{ik}$ in a suitable gauge. (b) Show that no gauge transformation brings it to the transverse-traceless form (13.84).
given: gauge freedom $h_{ik}\to h_{ik}-\partial_i\xi_k-\partial_k\xi_i$; Riemann tensor is gauge invariant

steps.reveal: $h_{tt}=\dfrac{2GM}{c^2r}$, $h_{ij}=\dfrac{2GM}{c^2r}\delta_{ij}$, $h_{ti}=0$ (from linearising Schwarzschild in isotropic coordinates); trace-reversed $\bar h_{tt}=4GM/c^2r$, others zero.
A TT field has only $h_{xx}=-h_{yy}$, $h_{xy}$, depending on $ct-x^3$: it has no $tt$ component and its Riemann tensor $R_{titj}$ is transverse and traceless.

The static field has $R_{titj}=\partial_i\partial_j\Phi/c^2$ with $\Phi=-GM/r$, whose trace $\nabla^2\Phi/c^2$ vanishes outside the star but which is not transverse (it has components along the radial direction) and does not oscillate. Since the Riemann tensor cannot be changed by gauge, no gauge makes $h$ TT: TT form is only possible for radiation, which obeys the vacuum wave equation with $\omega\neq0$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 13.7: No memory to linear order
enc.goal: A gravitational wave source emits for a finite time. A distant observer watches two free particles initially at rest. Show that after the wave has passed they are back at their original positions and at rest relative to each other (to linear order).
given: in TT gauge free particles stay at fixed coordinates; proper separation $L(t)=L_0\left(1+\frac12h_{ij}n^in^j\right)$

steps.prompt: Coordinates of free particles in TT gauge.
steps.reveal: The geodesic equation gives $\ddot x^i=-\Gamma^i_{tt}c^2=0$ in TT gauge (no $h_{tt}$, $h_{ti}$): they stay at fixed coordinates.
$L(t)=L_0+\frac12h_{ij}(t)n^in^jL_0$: it oscillates while the wave passes.

For a finite wave train $h_{ij}\to0$ again (linear theory, no static part), so $L\to L_0$ and $\dot L=\frac12\dot h_{ij}n^in^jL_0\to0$: same positions, relative rest. (A permanent offset, the nonlinear "memory effect", appears only at higher order.)

keyPoints: free particles at fixed TT coordinates

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.1: Scalar curvature of the 3-sphere and 3-hyperboloid
enc.goal: Find the scalar curvature of $ds^2=a^2[d\chi^2+\sin^2\chi(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)]$ and of the same metric with $\sinh\chi$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^\chi_{\theta\theta}=-\sin\chi\cos\chi$, $\Gamma^\chi_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\chi\cos\chi\sin^2\theta$, $\Gamma^\theta_{\chi\theta}=\Gamma^\phi_{\chi\phi}=\cot\chi$, $\Gamma^\theta_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\Gamma^\phi_{\theta\phi}=\cot\theta$.
$R_{\chi\chi}=2$, $R_{\theta\theta}=2\sin^2\chi$, $R_{\phi\phi}=2\sin^2\chi\sin^2\theta$, i.e. $R_{ij}=\dfrac2{a^2}g_{ij}$.
$R=g^{ij}R_{ij}=\dfrac{6}{a^2}$ for the 3-sphere, $-\dfrac6{a^2}$ for the hyperbolic space ($\sin\to\sinh$ flips the sign of $K$).
These are the spatial sections of the closed and open Robertson–Walker metrics with curvature $k/a^2$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.2: Ricci tensor of the Robertson–Walker metric
enc.goal: Calculate all components of $R_{ik}$ for the Robertson–Walker metric and verify (14.2): $R_{tt}=-3\dfrac{\ddot a}a$, $R_{\alpha\beta}=\left(\dfrac{\ddot a}a+2\dfrac{\dot a^2}{a^2}+2\dfrac{kc^2}{a^2}\right)\dfrac{g_{\alpha\beta}}{c^2}$.

steps.reveal: $\Gamma^t_{\alpha\beta}=\dfrac{a\dot a}{c^2}\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$, $\Gamma^\alpha_{t\beta}=\dfrac{\dot a}a\delta^\alpha_\beta$, plus the purely spatial $\Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\gamma}$ of $\gamma$.
$R_{tt}=-\partial_t\Gamma^\alpha_{t\alpha}-\Gamma^\alpha_{t\beta}\Gamma^\beta_{t\alpha}=-3\dfrac{d}{dt}\dfrac{\dot a}a-3\dfrac{\dot a^2}{a^2}=-3\dfrac{\ddot a}a$.

Time-derivative terms give $\dfrac{1}{c^2}(a\ddot a+2\dot a^2)\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$, the spatial curvature adds $2k\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$ (from Exercise 14.1); with $g_{\alpha\beta}=a^2\gamma_{\alpha\beta}$ that is (14.2).
With $T_{ik}$ of a perfect fluid, the $tt$ and $\alpha\beta$ components of Einstein’s equation give the Friedmann and acceleration equations.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.3: Instability of Einstein’s static universe
enc.goal: With a cosmological constant and $P=0$, let $a_0$ be the static solution. If $a$ is suddenly changed to $a_0+a_1$, show that $a_1$ grows exponentially.
given: $\ddot a=-\dfrac{4\pi G}3\rho a+\dfrac{\Lambda c^2}3a$, $\rho a^3=$ const

steps.reveal: $\ddot a=0\Rightarrow\Lambda c^2=4\pi G\rho_0$.
Write $\rho a=\rho_0a_0^3/a^2$: $\ddot a_1=\left[\dfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_0+\dfrac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\right]a_1=4\pi G\rho_0\,a_1$.

$a_1\propto e^{\pm\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_0}\,t}$: the growing mode wins. A slight expansion lowers the density, gravity weakens, $\Lambda$ wins and expansion accelerates (and vice versa): the static universe is unstable, which is why Einstein’s model could not describe the real Universe even before Hubble.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.4: Free particles slow down as $1/a$; decoupled relics
enc.goal: (a) For a free particle in the Robertson–Walker metric moving in $\chi$ only, show from the extremum of $\int ds$ that $a^2d\chi/d\tau$ is a constant, so the peculiar velocity decays as $a^{-1}$. (b) Particles in equilibrium while relativistic decouple and later become non-relativistic. Show that (11.7) keeps holding with $T\propto a^{-1}$. Is that $T$ a true temperature? Does (11.8) still hold? How do you find their density?

steps.reveal: The Lagrangian $\sqrt{c^2\dot t^2-a^2\dot\chi^2}$ does not contain $\chi$, so $a^2\,d\chi/d\tau$ is conserved. Peculiar velocity $v=a\,d\chi/dt$ with $\gamma v=a\,d\chi/d\tau\propto1/a$: momentum $\propto a^{-1}$, and for slow particles $v\propto a^{-1}$.

Every particle’s momentum scales as $p\propto1/a$ and the number in a comoving volume is fixed. The occupation number $f(p)=1/(e^{pc/\kappa_BT}\pm1)$ is conserved along the flow, so it keeps its form with $T\propto1/a$: (11.7) still holds.

It is only a parameter of the momentum distribution: the particles no longer interact, and once non-relativistic their energy is not $pc$, so the distribution is not Bose–Einstein or Fermi–Dirac in energy.

(11.8) fails because $E
eq pc$. Use $ho=mn$ with $n\propto a^{-3}$ fixed at decoupling: e.g. relic neutrinos with $n\approx113\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ per species give $\Omega_
u h^2=\sum m_
u/94$ eV.

keyPoints: distribution form preserved, $T$ only a parameter

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.5: Coordinate distance against redshift for $k=-1$
enc.goal: For $k=-1$ and $\Lambda=0$, derive the relation between coordinate distance $r$ and redshift $z$, and show it is the same as (14.32) for $k=+1$.

steps.reveal: $\sinh^{-1}r$; right side: $\displaystyle\int_0^z\frac{c\,dz}{a_0H_0\sqrt{\Omega_{M,0}(1+z)^3+(1-\Omega_{M,0})(1+z)^2}}$.

With $\Omega\equiv\Omega_{M,0}<1$ the integral is elementary (substitute $1+z=1/x$); taking $\sinh$ of the result gives (Mattig) $r=\dfrac{c}{a_0H_0}\dfrac{2\left[\Omega z+(2-\Omega)\left(1-\sqrt{1+\Omega z}\right)\right]}{\Omega^2(1+z)}$.

This is the same expression as for $k=+1$ (where $\sin^{-1}$ and $\sin$ appear instead): the curvature sign only enters through $a_0H_0$. Hence one formula holds for all $\Omega$, and it reduces to $r\,a_0H_0/c=2\left(1-1/\sqrt{1+z}\right)$ for $\Omega=1$.

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.6: Galaxy counts per redshift interval
enc.goal: If there are $n$ galaxies per unit comoving volume, find the number within solid angle $d\Omega$ with redshifts in $[z,z+dz]$.

steps.reveal: $dN=n\dfrac{a_0^3r^2}{\sqrt{1-kr^2}}\dfrac{dr}{dz}dz\,d\Omega$.
$\dfrac{dr}{\sqrt{1-kr^2}}=\dfrac{c\,dz}{a_0H(z)}$, so $dN=n\dfrac{c\,a_0^2r^2(z)}{H(z)}dz\,d\Omega$.

$a_0r=\dfrac{2c}{H_0}\left(1-\dfrac1{\sqrt{1+z}}\right)$, $H=H_0(1+z)^{3/2}$: $dN=n\left(\dfrac c{H_0}\right)^3\dfrac{4\left(1-(1+z)^{-1/2}\right)^2}{(1+z)^{3/2}}dz\,d\Omega$. The counts grow as $z^2$ at small $z$ and then turn over: number counts test the geometry (if galaxies did not evolve).

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.7: Standard candles: luminosity distance for three cosmologies
enc.goal: Using (14.51), numerically evaluate and plot the apparent luminosity of standard candles against $z$ for (i) $\Omega_M=1,\Omega_\Lambda=0$, (ii) $\Omega_M=0,\Omega_\Lambda=1$, (iii) $\Omega_M=0.3,\Omega_\Lambda=0.7$.

steps.prompt: All three are flat, so $S(x)\to x$.
steps.reveal: $d_L=(1+z)\dfrac c{H_0}\displaystyle\int_0^z\frac{dz'}{E(z')}$.

$l\propto d_L^{-2}$: at a given $z$ candles are faintest in the $\Lambda$-dominated model. At $z=0.5$, model (iii) is $(0.661/0.551)^2\approx1.44$ times fainter than EdS, i.e. 0.4 mag: what the 1998 supernova observations found (accelerating Universe).

enc.title: Choudhuri 14.8: Legendre coefficients of a Gaussian correlation function
enc.goal: For $C(\theta)=e^{-(\theta/\theta_0)^2}$ expanded as $C=\sum\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}C_lP_l(\cos\theta)$ (14.53), show $C_l=2\pi\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{+1}C(\theta)P_l(\cos\theta)\,d(\cos\theta)$. Write a code for the $C_l$, run it for a few $\theta_0$ and find the $l$ where $C_l$ is maximum.
given: Note: Our text copy asks for the maximum of $C_l$; for a Gaussian that is $l=0$, so the useful statement is the peak of $l(l+1)C_l$, as plotted for the CMB.

steps.reveal: Multiply (14.53) by $P_{l'}(\cos\theta)$ and integrate over $x=\cos\theta$: $\int CP_{l'}dx=\frac{2l'+1}{4\pi}C_{l'}\frac2{2l'+1}=\frac{C_{l'}}{2\pi}$, so $C_l=2\pi\int_{-1}^1CP_l\,dx$.

Integrate $2\pi\int_0^\pi e^{-(\theta/\theta_0)^2}P_l(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta$ (only $\theta\lesssim5\theta_0$ matters), with $P_l$ from the recurrence $(l+1)P_{l+1}=(2l+1)xP_l-lP_{l-1}$, for $l=0\ldots10/\theta_0$.

For small $\theta_0$, $C_l\approx\pi\theta_0^2e^{-l(l+1)\theta_0^2/4}$: $C_l$ itself is largest at $l=0$ and decreases. The quantity plotted for the CMB, $l(l+1)C_l$, peaks at $l\approx2/\theta_0$: computed $l=114$, $22$, $11$ for $\theta_0=1^\circ,5^\circ,10^\circ$ (prediction $115$, $22.9$, $11.5$).
Structure of angular size $\theta$ shows up at $l\sim\pi/\theta$: the first acoustic peak at $l\approx200$ corresponds to $\approx1^\circ$, the sound horizon at recombination seen in a flat Universe.
